\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The object}
A \emph{Pythagorean triple} is a triple $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers with
$a^2+b^2=c^2$; it is \emph{primitive} if $\gcd(a,b)=1$. Since $\gcd(a,b)=1$
forces $\gcd(a,c)=\gcd(b,c)=1$, primitivity says equivalently that no integer
$>1$ divides all three coordinates.

The set of primitive triples has two classical descriptions. The \emph{Euclid
parametrisation} says that every primitive triple with odd first leg equals
$(m^2-n^2,\,2mn,\,m^2+n^2)$ for a unique pair $0<n<m$ with $\gcd(n,m)=1$ and
$n+m$ odd. The \emph{Berggren description}, found by B.~Berggren in 1934 and
rediscovered several times since, is structural rather than parametric: the
three integer matrices
\[
B_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_3 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix},
\]
acting on column vectors and applied repeatedly to the seed $(3,4,5)$, generate
every primitive triple with odd first leg exactly once.

\subsection{The question}
Both descriptions are qualitative. We ask: how many of the $H^3$ integer points
of the box $[1,H]^3$ are Berggren-generated, and how does that count compare
with the number of primitive Pythagorean triples in the same box? The answers
proved below are $\Theta(H)$ --- hence a vanishing proportion of $H^3$ --- and
\emph{exactly one half} of the ordered primitive triples, i.e.\ all of them once
the legs are regarded as unordered.

\section{Notation}

\begin{definition}[Triple, validity]
A \emph{triple} is $t=(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$. It is \textbf{valid} if
\[
a>0,\quad b>0,\quad c>0,\quad a^2+b^2=c^2,\quad \gcd(a,b)=1,\quad a\equiv1\!\!\pmod 2 .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The Berggren maps]
Define $\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb Z^3$ by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_1(a,b,c) &= (\,a-2b+2c,\ \ 2a-b+2c,\ \ 2a-2b+3c\,),\\
\beta_2(a,b,c) &= (\,a+2b+2c,\ \ 2a+b+2c,\ \ 2a+2b+3c\,),\\
\beta_3(a,b,c) &= (-a+2b+2c,\ -2a+b+2c,\ -2a+2b+3c\,),
\end{aligned}
\]
the actions of $B_1,B_2,B_3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The tree]
The \emph{Berggren tree} $\Tt$ is the smallest subset of $\mathbb Z^3$
containing $(3,4,5)$ and closed under $\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3$. Equivalently
$t\in\Tt$ iff $t=\rho(w):=\beta_{w_1}\cdots\beta_{w_\ell}(3,4,5)$ for some word
$w\in\{1,2,3\}^{\ell}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The boxes]
For $H\in\mathbb N$ set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Bx(H) &= \{\,t\in\Tt : 1\le a,b,c\le H\,\},\\
\Pp(H) &= \{\,(a,b,c) : 1\le a,b,c\le H,\ a^2+b^2=c^2,\ \gcd(a,b)=1\,\},\\
\Pp^{\mathrm{odd}}(H) &= \{\,t\in\Pp(H) : a \text{ odd}\,\},\\
\Qq(H) &= \{\,(n,m) : 1\le n<m,\ \gcd(n,m)=1,\ n+m \text{ odd},\ m^2+n^2\le H\,\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $\Pp(H)$ counts \emph{ordered} triples.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[The box condition is a hypotenuse condition]\label{rem:hyp}
For a positive Pythagorean triple, $a<c$ and $b<c$. Hence $t\in\Bx(H)$ iff
$t\in\Tt$ and $c\le H$, and likewise for $\Pp(H)$.
\end{remark}

\section{The structure theorem}

\subsection{Closure}

\begin{lemma}[Each generator preserves validity]\label{lem:closure}
If $t$ is valid then so are $\beta_1(t),\beta_2(t),\beta_3(t)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Four checks per generator.
\emph{(i) Pythagorean identity:} e.g.
$(a+2b+2c)^2+(2a+b+2c)^2-(2a+2b+3c)^2 = -a^2-b^2+c^2 = 0$,
a polynomial identity modulo $a^2+b^2=c^2$; similarly for $\beta_1,\beta_3$.
\emph{(ii) Positivity:} for a positive Pythagorean triple $c<a+b$ (square:
$c^2=a^2+b^2<(a+b)^2$) and $a,b<c$; substituting these into each coordinate
makes it a positive combination.
\emph{(iii) Primitivity:} each $B_i$ has determinant $\pm1$, so $B_i^{-1}$ is
integral; a common divisor of the image coordinates divides the source
coordinates and conversely.
\emph{(iv) Parity:} if $a$ is odd then $b$ is even and $c$ is odd
(Lemma~\ref{lem:parity}), so $\pm a+2b+2c$ is odd.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Closure]\label{thm:closure}
Every $t\in\Tt$ is valid.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the generation of $\Tt$; the seed is valid and
Lemma~\ref{lem:closure} propagates validity.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Completeness by descent}

For a valid triple $(a,b,c)$ define the \emph{parent forms}
\[
u = a+2b-2c, \qquad v = 2a+b-2c, \qquad w = 3c-2a-2b .
\]
They are the coordinates read off by the inverse matrices: for each $i$ there
are signs with $B_i^{-1}(a,b,c) = (\varepsilon_i u, \delta_i v, w)$, namely
$(\varepsilon,\delta)=(+,-)$ for $B_1$, $(+,+)$ for $B_2$, $(-,+)$ for $B_3$.

\begin{lemma}[The parent hypotenuse strictly decreases]\label{lem:w}
For a positive Pythagorean triple, $0<w<c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$w<c$ is $c<a+b$, proved above. For $w>0$ we need $2(a+b)<3c$: squaring,
$4(a+b)^2 = 4(c^2+2ab)\le 8c^2 < 9c^2$, using $2ab\le a^2+b^2=c^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sign dichotomy]\label{lem:sign}
For a valid triple, $u$ and $v$ are not both $\le0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $u\le0$, i.e.\ $a\le 2(c-b)$; since $b<c$ the right-hand side is
positive, so we may square: $c^2-b^2 = a^2 \le 4(c-b)^2$. Dividing by $c-b>0$
gives $c+b\le 4(c-b)$, i.e.\ $5b\le 3c$. Symmetrically $v\le0$ gives $5a\le3c$.
If both held, $25c^2 = 25(a^2+b^2)\le 18c^2$, absurd.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Degenerate forms]\label{lem:degen}
For a valid triple, $u\ne0$; and $v=0$ if and only if $(a,b,c)=(3,4,5)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $u=0$ then $a=2(c-b)$ is even, contradicting oddness. If $v=0$ then
$b=2(c-a)$, and $a^2+4(c-a)^2=c^2$ factors as $(5a-3c)(a-c)=0$; since $a<c$ we
get $5a=3c$, and primitivity pins $(a,b,c)=(3,4,5)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The parent is valid]\label{lem:parent}
Let $(a,b,c)$ be valid and not the seed, and set $\varepsilon=\sgn u$,
$\delta=\sgn v$. Then $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ is one of the three admissible
patterns $(+,-),(+,+),(-,+)$, the triple $p=(\varepsilon u,\delta v,w)$ is
valid, and $\beta_i(p)=(a,b,c)$ for the corresponding index $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$u^2+v^2=w^2$ is a polynomial identity modulo $a^2+b^2=c^2$; positivity of
$|u|,|v|,w$ is Lemmas~\ref{lem:w}--\ref{lem:degen}; primitivity transfers
backwards by unimodularity; $\varepsilon u\equiv a \equiv 1 \pmod 2$; and
$B_iB_i^{-1}=I$ gives $\beta_i(p)=(a,b,c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness]\label{thm:complete}
Every valid triple lies in $\Tt$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $c$. If $(a,b,c)=(3,4,5)$ it is the seed; otherwise
Lemma~\ref{lem:parent} gives a valid parent with hypotenuse $w<c$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:w}), which lies in $\Tt$ by induction, and one application of
$\beta_i$ returns $(a,b,c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Berggren's theorem, effective form]\label{thm:berggren}
$t\in\Tt$ if and only if $t$ is valid.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Freeness}

\begin{theorem}[Freeness]\label{thm:free}
The word map $\rho$ is injective: distinct words give distinct triples, so
$\Tt$ is a free ternary tree and every valid triple has a unique address.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Two ingredients. \emph{(a)} The forms $u,v$ satisfy
$u(\beta_1t)=u(\beta_2t)=a$, $u(\beta_3t)=-a$, $v(\beta_1t)=-b$,
$v(\beta_2t)=v(\beta_3t)=b$, so the sign pattern $(\sgn u,\sgn v)$ of an image
determines which generator produced it (using $a,b>0$); each $\beta_i$ is
individually injective by unimodularity. \emph{(b)} For valid $p$, every
$\beta_i(p)$ has hypotenuse $>5$, so the root is not a child. Induct on word
length.
\end{proof}

\section{The upper bound}

\begin{lemma}[Two-square decomposition]\label{lem:twosq}
If $t=(a,b,c)$ is valid then there are integers $M,N\ge0$ with
$c+a = 2M^2$ and $c-a = 2N^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By the classification of coprime Pythagorean triples, $a=\pm(m^2-n^2)$,
$b=\pm2mn$, $c=\pm(m^2+n^2)$ for integers $m,n$. Positivity forces
$c=m^2+n^2$, and oddness of $a$ forces the branch $a=m^2-n^2$ (the alternative
$a=2mn$ is even). Then $c+a=2m^2$ and $c-a=2n^2$; take $M=|m|,N=|n|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp upper bound]\label{thm:upper}
For every $H$, $\ \#\Bx(H) \le (\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor+1)^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\Phi(a,b,c) = (c+a,\,c-a)$. It is injective on $\Bx(H)$: from $c+a$ and
$c-a$ one recovers $a,c$, and then $b>0$ is determined by $b^2=c^2-a^2$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:twosq}, $\Phi(t) = (2M^2,2N^2)$, and $a<c\le H$ gives
$2M^2 = c+a\le 2H$ and $2N^2 = c-a \le 2H$, so $M,N\le\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor$.
Hence $\Phi(\Bx(H))$ lies in the image of
$\{0,\dots,\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor\}^2$ under $(M,N)\mapsto(2M^2,2N^2)$, a set of
at most $(\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor+1)^2$ elements.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Linear upper bound]\label{cor:4H}
For $H\ge1$, $\ \#\Bx(H)\le 4H$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
With $s=\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor\ge1$ and $s^2\le H$:
$(s+1)^2 = s^2+2s+1 \le 4s^2 \le 4H$.
\end{proof}

\section{The lower bound}

Let $S(X)=\{1,\dots,X\}^2$ and $\Cop(X)=\{(n,m)\in S(X):\gcd(n,m)=1\}$.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary sieve]\label{lem:sieve}
$\#\bigl(S(X)\setminus\Cop(X)\bigr) \le \sum_{g=2}^{X}\lfloor X/g\rfloor^2 .$
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $\gcd(n,m)=g>1$ then $(n,m)=g\cdot(n',m')$ with $1\le n',m'\le\lfloor X/g\rfloor$;
summing over $g$ overcounts.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tail estimate]\label{lem:tail}
$\sum_{g\ge2} 1/g^2 \le 25/36 .$
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $g=2,3$ exactly ($\tfrac14+\tfrac19=\tfrac{13}{36}$) and telescope the
tail: $\sum_{g\ge4}1/g^2 \le \sum_{g\ge4}\tfrac{1}{g(g-1)} = \tfrac13$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Effective coprime density]\label{prop:cop}
$11X^2 \le 36\,\#\Cop(X)$: at least $11/36=0.3055\ldots$ of the pairs in
$[1,X]^2$ are coprime. (The truth is $6/\pi^2 = 0.6079\ldots$.)
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Ordering and parity]\label{prop:parity}
Let $\Cop^{<}(X)$ be the coprime pairs with $n<m$, and $\Cop^{\ne}(X)$ those
also of opposite parity. Then
\[
\#\Cop(X)\le 2\,\#\Cop^{<}(X)+1, \qquad \#\Cop^{<}(X)\le 2\,\#\Cop^{\ne}(X),
\]
whence $11X^2 \le 144\,\#\Cop^{\ne}(X)+36$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first bound is the involution $(n,m)\mapsto(m,n)$, whose only coprime fixed
point is $(1,1)$. For the second, if $n<m$ are coprime and both odd then
$\bigl(\tfrac{m-n}{2},\tfrac{m+n}{2}\bigr)$ is a coprime opposite-parity pair
with entries in $[1,X]$ and first entry smaller; the map is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Euclid's map produces valid triples]\label{lem:euclid}
If $1\le n<m$, $\gcd(n,m)=1$ and $n+m$ is odd then
$E(n,m):=(m^2-n^2,\,2mn,\,m^2+n^2)$ is valid.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound]\label{thm:lower}
For $H\ge5$, $\ H \le 100\,\#\Bx(H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $X=\lfloor\sqrt{\lfloor H/2\rfloor}\rfloor \ge 1$. For
$(n,m)\in\Cop^{\ne}(X)$ we have $m^2+n^2\le 2X^2\le H$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:euclid} and Theorem~\ref{thm:berggren} the triple $E(n,m)$ is a
tree triple with hypotenuse $\le H$, hence in $\Bx(H)$ by
Remark~\ref{rem:hyp}. The map $E$ is injective (from $m^2\pm n^2$ recover
$m,n>0$), so $\#\Cop^{\ne}(X)\le \#\Bx(H)$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:parity} gives $11X^2 \le 144\,\#\Bx(H)+36$. Moreover
$\lfloor H/2\rfloor<(X+1)^2\le 4X^2$, so $H \le 2\lfloor H/2\rfloor+1\le 8X^2+1$,
and $\#\Bx(H)\ge1$ since $(3,4,5)\in\Bx(H)$. Combining the three gives
$H\le100\,\#\Bx(H)$.
\end{proof}

The constant $100$ is not optimised; it collects the losses $\tfrac{36}{11}$
(coprimality), $2$ (ordering), $2$ (parity), $2$ (square inscribed in the disc)
and rounding.

\section{$\Theta(H)$ and vanishing density}

\begin{theorem}[Main counting theorem]\label{thm:main}
For all $H\ge5$,
\[
\frac{H}{100} \;\le\; \#\Bx(H) \;\le\; \min\bigl(4H,\ (\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor+1)^2\bigr),
\]
so $\#\Bx(H)=\Theta(H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Vanishing density in the box]\label{cor:density}
$\#\Bx(H)/H^3 \le 4/H$ for $H\ge1$, hence $\lim_{H\to\infty}\#\Bx(H)/H^3=0$.
\end{corollary}

Choosing a lattice point uniformly at random from $[1,H]^3$, the probability of
landing on a Berggren triple is $O(1/H^2)$.

\section{Exact comparison with the primitive Pythagorean triples}

\begin{lemma}[Parity of a primitive triple]\label{lem:parity}
In a primitive Pythagorean triple, exactly one leg is odd, and $c$ is odd.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both legs even is excluded by $\gcd(a,b)=1$. If both are odd, then
$c^2=a^2+b^2\equiv2\pmod4$, impossible since squares are $0$ or $1$ mod $4$.
Hence exactly one leg is odd and $c^2$ is odd.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The tree is exactly the odd-first-leg primitive triples]\label{thm:odd}
$\Bx(H)=\Pp^{\mathrm{odd}}(H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\subseteq$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}; $\supseteq$ is
Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}, since a member of $\Pp^{\mathrm{odd}}(H)$ is exactly
a valid triple lying in the box.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The factor two]\label{thm:two}
For every $H$, $\ \#\Pp(H) = 2\,\#\Bx(H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Split $\Pp(H)$ by the parity of the first coordinate. The leg swap
$\sigma(a,b,c)=(b,a,c)$ maps $\Pp(H)$ to itself, is an involution, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:parity} exchanges the odd-first-leg and even-first-leg parts;
hence they are equinumerous, and Theorem~\ref{thm:odd} finishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Completeness in the box, up to a swap]\label{cor:swap}
For every $(a,b,c)\in\Pp(H)$, either $(a,b,c)\in\Bx(H)$ or $(b,a,c)\in\Bx(H)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Corollary~\ref{cor:swap} is the sharp form of the heuristic that the tree
captures a $(1-o(1))$ proportion of the primitive triples of the box: the
proportion is exactly $1$. Viewed as a set of right \emph{triangles}, with the
legs unordered, the tree restricted to the box \emph{is} the set of all
primitive Pythagorean triangles of hypotenuse at most $H$.
\end{remark}

\section{The visible-point bijection and the constant $1/(2\pi)$}

\begin{theorem}[Bijection with the parameter wedge]\label{thm:bij}
The Euclid map $E(n,m)=(m^2-n^2,\,2mn,\,m^2+n^2)$ is a bijection
$\Qq(H)\to\Bx(H)$. Hence $\#\Bx(H)=\#\Qq(H)$ and $\#\Pp(H)=2\,\#\Qq(H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Well-definedness is Lemma~\ref{lem:euclid} plus Remark~\ref{rem:hyp}.
Injectivity: $m^2 = \tfrac12((m^2+n^2)+(m^2-n^2))$ and
$n^2 = \tfrac12((m^2+n^2)-(m^2-n^2))$. Surjectivity: given $t\in\Bx(H)$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:twosq} gives $M,N$ with $c+a=2M^2$, $c-a=2N^2$; then
$c=M^2+N^2\le H$, $a=M^2-N^2>0$ so $N<M$, $b^2=c^2-a^2=(2MN)^2$ so $b=2MN$ and
$N\ge1$; $\gcd(a,b)=1$ forces $\gcd(N,M)=1$, and $a$ odd forces $N+M$ odd.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bij} converts a question about a three-dimensional orbit of a
matrix semigroup into a count of \emph{visible} lattice points --- points seen
from the origin with no lattice point in between --- inside the circular wedge
$W_H=\{(x,y):0<x<y,\ x^2+y^2\le H\}$, subject to a parity condition.

\subsection{The predicted constant}
The wedge $W_H$ is an eighth of a disc of radius $\sqrt H$, of area $\pi H/8$.
Three densities act on its lattice points:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Area:} $\#(\mathbb Z^2\cap W_H) = \pi H/8 + O(\sqrt H)$, by the
Gauss circle argument.
\item \textbf{Visibility:} coprime pairs have density $1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$, by
Möbius inversion.
\item \textbf{Parity:} among coprime pairs the classes
(odd,\,odd), (odd,\,even), (even,\,odd) are equidistributed, so exactly $2/3$
have opposite parity --- the local factor at the prime $2$ in the sieve is
$\tfrac{2/4}{3/4}=\tfrac23$.
\end{enumerate}
Multiplying, $\#\Qq(H) \sim \tfrac{\pi H}{8}\cdot\tfrac{6}{\pi^2}\cdot\tfrac23 = \tfrac{H}{2\pi}$.

\begin{conjecture}[Lehmer-type constant for the Berggren box]\label{conj}
$\#\Bx(H) = \dfrac{H}{2\pi} + O(\sqrt H\log H)$; in particular
$\#\Bx(H)/H\to 1/(2\pi) = 0.1591549\ldots$
\end{conjecture}

At $H=4\cdot10^5$ one finds $\#\Bx(H) = 63\,669$ and $\#\Bx(H)/H = 0.159172$
against $1/(2\pi) = 0.159155$, a discrepancy consistent with an $O(\sqrt H)$
error term. Note that the proved bounds give $1/100 \le \#\Bx(H)/H \le 1$; the
upper bound is off by exactly $2\pi$, which is precisely the geometric content
discarded by the two-square argument.

\section{Growth geometry of the generators}

\subsection{The hyperbolic generator}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:hyp}
If $t=(a,b,c)$ is valid then $(\beta_2t)_3 > 5c$; hence
$(\beta_2^{\,k}t)_3 \ge 5^kc$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$(\beta_2t)_3 = 2a+2b+3c > 2c+3c = 5c$, using $a+b>c$; iterate.
\end{proof}

The exact expansion factor is the largest eigenvalue of $B_2$, the silver-ratio
square $3+2\sqrt2 = 5.8284\ldots$. From $(3,4,5)$ the pure-$B_2$ branch has
hypotenuses $5,29,169,985,5741,33461,195025,\dots$ (alternate Pell numbers),
carrying the triples whose legs differ by one.

\subsection{The parabolic generator}

$B_3$ is unipotent, with characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-1)^3$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:inv}
$(\beta_3t)_3-(\beta_3t)_1 = c-a$ for every $t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Closed form for the parabolic orbit]\label{thm:orbit}
For every $k\ge0$ and $t=(a,b,c)$, with $\gamma=-2a+2b+2c$,
\[
\beta_3^{\,k}(t) = \bigl(a+k\gamma+2k(k-1)(c-a),\ \ b+2k(c-a),\ \ c+k\gamma+2k(k-1)(c-a)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

Thus the hypotenuse grows \emph{quadratically} along a $B_3$ orbit. From the
seed this is the \emph{parabolic spine}
\[
\beta_3^{\,k}(3,4,5) = \bigl(4(k+1)^2-1,\ 4(k+1),\ 4(k+1)^2+1\bigr),
\]
i.e.\ $(3,4,5),(15,8,17),(35,12,37),(63,16,65),(99,20,101),\dots$: the triples
with $c-a=2$.

\begin{theorem}[Seed-independent depth bound]\label{thm:depth}
Let $t$ be valid with hypotenuse $c$, and let $7K^2c\le H$. Then
$\{t,\beta_3t,\dots,\beta_3^{K-1}t\}$ consists of $K$ distinct valid triples
inside $[1,H]^3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The hypotenuse strictly increases along the orbit (Theorem~\ref{thm:orbit} with
$\gamma>0$, $c>a$), giving distinctness; and $\gamma\le4c$, $c-a\le c$ give
$(\beta_3^{\,k}t)_3 \le 7(k+1)^2c \le 7K^2c \le H$ for $k<K$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A uniform depth bound}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:uniform}
For a word $w$ of length $d$, $\rho(w)$ has hypotenuse at most $5\cdot6^{d}$;
equivalently a triple with hypotenuse $c$ sits at depth $\ge\log_6(c/5)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2(a+b)\le3c$ for a valid triple (Lemma~\ref{lem:w}), so each generator's third
coordinate is at most $2(a+b)+3c\le6c$; iterate from the seed hypotenuse $5$.
\end{proof}

Depths inside the box therefore range from $\Theta(\log H)$ in the
exponentially branching bulk to $\Omega(\sqrt H)$ along parabolic whiskers.
Empirically, at $H=10^5$ the tree has $15\,919$ nodes of mean depth $15.4$ and
maximum depth $222$.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Enumeration via the tree}
By Remark~\ref{rem:hyp} the box condition is $c\le H$, and every generator
strictly increases $c$; so a depth-first search from $(3,4,5)$ pruned at $c>H$
enumerates $\Bx(H)$ exactly once each, in $O(\#\Bx(H))=O(H)$ operations and
$O(\text{depth})$ space, with no duplicate detection needed by
Theorem~\ref{thm:free}.

\subsection{Enumeration via the parameter wedge}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:bij}, loop over $2\le m\le\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor$ and
$1\le n<m$ with $m^2+n^2\le H$, keeping $\gcd(n,m)=1$ and $n+m$ odd; cost
$O(H\log H)$.

\subsection{Address of a triple}
Iterate the descent: if $t=(3,4,5)$ stop; else compute $u,v,w$, read the
generator index from $(\sgn u,\sgn v)$, and replace $t$ by $(|u|,|v|,w)$. This
recovers the unique word $\rho^{-1}(t)$.

\subsection{Sieved counting}
Möbius inversion over the visibility condition gives
\[
\#\Qq(H) = \sum_{d\ \mathrm{odd}} \mu(d)\,
\#\{(n,m): 0<n<m,\ n+m \text{ odd},\ d\mid n,\ d\mid m,\ m^2+n^2\le H\},
\]
only odd $d$ contributing (even $d$ would force both entries even). Each inner
count is a wedge count of radius $\sqrt H/d$, computable in $O(\sqrt H/d)$ time,
for a total of $O(\sqrt H\log H)$.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Three answers to one question}
``How common are Pythagorean triples?'' has three sharp and different answers:
in the box $[1,H]^3$ they are a proportion $O(1/H^2)$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:density}); per unit of height there are exactly $\Theta(H)$
of them, conjecturally $H/(2\pi)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:main},
Conjecture~\ref{conj}); and among primitive Pythagorean triples the tree
captures all of them, up to a leg swap (Corollary~\ref{cor:swap}). The tension
dissolves once one notes that these compare the tree against three different
ambient sets.

\subsection{Where the constants are lost}
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} brackets $\#\Bx(H)/H$ in $[1/100,1]$ while the truth is
$0.159$. The upper bound discards the \emph{shape} of the constraint region
(bounding the wedge by the full square: a factor $8/\pi$), the coprimality
condition ($\pi^2/6$) and the parity condition ($3/2$); their product is exactly
$2\pi$. On the lower side, the losses are the elementary sieve ($36/11$ instead
of $\pi^2/6$), the two symmetry factors, and the square-in-disc inscription.

\subsection{Open problems}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove Conjecture~\ref{conj}: the bijection is exact, so what remains is a
Möbius-weighted Gauss circle estimate for the wedge, requiring uniform control
of the lattice-point discrepancy for discs of radius $\sqrt H/d$ summed against
$\mu(d)$.
\item Sharpen the effective constants: an effective Möbius argument in place of
Proposition~\ref{prop:cop} should narrow $[1/100,1]$ to roughly $[0.14,0.18]$.
\item Determine the depth profile: prove $D(H)\asymp\sqrt H$ for the maximal
depth inside the box (the lower bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:depth}) and
$\Theta(\log H)$ for the typical depth.
\item Classify other free covering trees: which triples of unimodular matrices
generate a free tree covering a Diophantine set, and does the
$\Theta(H)$-with-computable-constant phenomenon persist?
\item Count by perimeter or area instead of hypotenuse: the wedge is replaced by
a hyperbola-bounded region and the constant by a corresponding integral.
\item Higher-dimensional analogues: quaternionic trees generating primitive
quadruples $a^2+b^2+c^2=d^2$ should give box counts $\Theta(H^2)$ with a
constant coming from a spherical shell.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Summary of results}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Structure.} The Berggren tree rooted at $(3,4,5)$ equals the set
of positive primitive Pythagorean triples with odd first leg, and is free.
\item \textbf{Upper bound.} $\#\Bx(H)\le(\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor+1)^2\le4H$.
\item \textbf{Lower bound.} $H\le100\,\#\Bx(H)$ for $H\ge5$.
\item \textbf{Order of growth.} $\#\Bx(H)=\Theta(H)$ and $\#\Bx(H)/H^3\to0$.
\item \textbf{Exact comparison.} $\#\Pp(H)=2\,\#\Bx(H)$, and every primitive
Pythagorean triple of the box is in the tree up to a leg swap.
\item \textbf{Reduction.} $\#\Bx(H)=\#\Qq(H)$, a visible-point count in a
circular wedge, whence the conjectural constant $1/(2\pi)$.
\item \textbf{Geometry.} $B_2$ expands the hypotenuse by $3+2\sqrt2$; $B_3$ is
unipotent with quadratic orbit growth $c_k=4(k+1)^2+1$ from the seed, forcing
depth $\Omega(\sqrt H)$ inside the box against a generic depth $\Theta(\log H)$.
\end{itemize}

    primitive Pythagorean triples in the box.  Hence the tree captures every
    primitive triple of the box up to swapping the two legs: the advertised
    proportion "1 - o(1)" is in fact exactly 1.

  * #bergBox(H) = #pairBox(H), the number of coprime, opposite-parity lattice
    points (n,m) with 0 < n < m and m^2 + n^2 <= H (a "visible point" count in a
    quarter disc).  Experimentally #bergBox(H)/H -> 1/(2*pi) = 0.159154...

Run:  python3 demo.py

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from math import gcd, isqrt, pi
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1. The three Berggren matrices
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

B1: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
B2: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
B3: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))

SEED: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


def apply_matrix(matrix: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...], t: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to a triple, returning the image triple."""
    a, b, c = t
    return tuple(row[0] * a + row[1] * b + row[2] * c for row in matrix)  # type: ignore[return-value]


def children(t: Triple) -> List[Triple]:
    """The three Berggren children of a triple."""
    return [apply_matrix(B1, t), apply_matrix(B2, t), apply_matrix(B3, t)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 2. Enumerating the tree inside a box
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def berg_box(H: int) -> List[Triple]:
    """All Berggren-generated triples (a,b,c) with 0 < a,b,c <= H.

    Because c > a and c > b for a Pythagorean triple, the box condition is just
    c <= H; and every Berggren step strictly increases c, so a depth-first search
    pruned at c > H is complete.
    """
    out: List[Triple] = []
    stack: List[Triple] = [SEED]
    while stack:
        t = stack.pop()
        if t[2] > H:
            continue
        out.append(t)
        stack.extend(children(t))
    return sorted(out)


def pp_box(H: int) -> List[Triple]:
    """All ordered primitive Pythagorean triples (a,b,c) with 0 < a,b,c <= H."""
    out: List[Triple] = []
    for c in range(1, H + 1):
        for a in range(1, c):
            b2 = c * c - a * a
            b = isqrt(b2)
            if b * b == b2 and 0 < b <= H and gcd(a, b) == 1:
                out.append((a, b, c))
    return sorted(out)


def pair_box(H: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Coprime opposite-parity pairs (n,m), 0 < n < m, with m^2 + n^2 <= H."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    mmax = isqrt(H)
    for m in range(2, mmax + 1):
        for n in range(1, m):
            if m * m + n * n <= H and gcd(n, m) == 1 and (n + m) % 2 == 1:
                out.append((n, m))
    return sorted(out)


def euclid(n: int, m: int) -> Triple:
    """Euclid's parametrisation: (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2)."""
    return (m * m - n * n, 2 * m * n, m * m + n * n)

# 3. Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def apply_matrix(matrix: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...], t: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to a triple, returning the image triple."""
    a, b, c = t

def berg_box(H: int) -> List[Triple]:
    """All Berggren-generated triples (a,b,c) with 0 < a,b,c <= H.

    while stack:

    return sorted(out)

    """All ordered primitive Pythagorean triples (a,b,c) with 0 < a,b,c <= H."""

    for c in range(1, H + 1):

            b = isqrt(b2)

from __future__ import annotations

import time
from math import gcd, isqrt, pi
from typing import List


def mobius_table(N: int) -> List[int]:
    """The Moebius function on 1..N by a sieve of Eratosthenes type."""
    mu = [1] * (N + 1)
    primes: List[int] = []
    is_comp = [False] * (N + 1)
    for i in range(2, N + 1):
        if not is_comp[i]:
            primes.append(i)
            mu[i] = -1
        for p in primes:
            if i * p > N:
                break
            is_comp[i * p] = True
            if i % p == 0:
                mu[i * p] = 0
                break
            mu[i * p] = -mu[i]
    return mu


def wedge_opposite_parity(T: int) -> int:
    """A(T) = #{(n,m) : 0 < n < m, n+m odd, m^2+n^2 <= T}, in O(sqrt(T))."""
    total = 0
    for m in range(2, isqrt(T) + 1):
        nmax = min(m - 1, isqrt(T - m * m))
        if nmax < 1:
            continue
        total += (nmax + 1) // 2 if m % 2 == 0 else nmax // 2
    return total


def count_sieved(H: int) -> int:
    """#B(H) in O(sqrt(H) log H) time and O(sqrt(H)) memory."""
    D = isqrt(H)
    mu = mobius_table(max(D, 1))
    return sum(mu[d] * wedge_opposite_parity(H // (d * d))
               for d in range(1, D + 1, 2) if mu[d])

    """#B(H) by direct enumeration of the wedge, for cross-checking.  O(H)."""
    total = 0

        for n in range(1, m):
            if m * m + n * n > H:
                break
            if gcd(n, m) == 1 and (n + m) % 2 == 1:
                total += 1
    return total

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]

B1 = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
B2 = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
B3 = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))
SEED: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


def apply_matrix(matrix: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...], t: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to the column vector (a, b, c)."""
    a, b, c = t
    return (
        matrix[0][0] * a + matrix[0][1] * b + matrix[0][2] * c,
        matrix[1][0] * a + matrix[1][1] * b + matrix[1][2] * c,
        matrix[2][0] * a + matrix[2][1] * b + matrix[2][2] * c,
    )


def berggren_box(H: int) -> Iterator[Triple]:
    """Yield every Berggren-generated triple (a, b, c) with 0 < a, b, c <= H.

    Correctness rests on two facts proved in the paper:
      * for a Pythagorean triple, a < c and b < c, so the box condition on the
        three coordinates reduces to the single condition c <= H;
      * every generator strictly increases the hypotenuse, so pruning a node
        with c > H discards only nodes whose whole subtree lies outside the box.
    Freeness of the tree guarantees each triple is emitted exactly once, so no
    duplicate detection is required.

    Complexity: O(#output) = O(H) arithmetic operations, O(depth) space.
    """
    stack: List[Triple] = [SEED]
    while stack:
        t = stack.pop()
        if t[2] > H:
            continue
        yield t
        stack.append(apply_matrix(B1, t))
        stack.append(apply_matrix(B2, t))
        stack.append(apply_matrix(B3, t))


def count_berggren_box(H: int) -> int:
    """The cardinality #B(H); satisfies H/100 <= #B(H) <= min(4H, (isqrt(H)+1)^2)."""
    return sum(1 for _ in berggren_box(H))

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]

SEED: Triple = (3, 4, 5)

B1 = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
B2 = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
B3 = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))
MATRICES = {1: B1, 2: B2, 3: B3}


def is_valid(t: Triple) -> bool:
    """Positive primitive Pythagorean triple with odd first leg."""
    a, b, c = t
    return (a > 0 and b > 0 and c > 0 and a * a + b * b == c * c
            and gcd(a, b) == 1 and a % 2 == 1)


def parent(t: Triple) -> Tuple[int, Triple]:
    """One descent step.

    For a valid triple (a, b, c) other than the seed, the three parent forms

        u = a + 2b - 2c,   v = 2a + b - 2c,   w = 3c - 2a - 2b

    satisfy 0 < w < c, u != 0, and (u, v) is never in the third quadrant.  The
    sign pattern (sgn u, sgn v) selects the unique generator that produced t:

        (+, -) -> B1,   (+, +) -> B2,   (-, +) -> B3,

    and the parent is (|u|, |v|, w), again a valid triple.  Returns the index of
    the generator and the parent triple.
    """
    a, b, c = t
    u = a + 2 * b - 2 * c
    v = 2 * a + b - 2 * c
    w = 3 * c - 2 * a - 2 * b
    if u > 0 and v < 0:
        idx = 1
    elif u > 0 and v > 0:
        idx = 2
    elif u < 0 and v > 0:
        idx = 3
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"degenerate sign pattern for {t}: u={u}, v={v}")
    return idx, (abs(u), abs(v), w)


def address(t: Triple) -> List[int]:
    """The unique word w in {1,2,3}* with beta_w(3,4,5) = t, outermost last.

    The hypotenuse strictly decreases at every step, so the loop terminates.
    Length is at most log_6(c/5) on hyperbolic branches and O(sqrt(c)) in the
    worst (parabolic) case; each step is O(1) arithmetic.
    """
    if not is_valid(t):
        raise ValueError(f"{t} is not a positive primitive triple with odd first leg")
    word: List[int] = []
    while t != SEED:
        idx, t = parent(t)
        word.append(idx)
    return word


def rebuild(word: List[int]) -> Triple:
    """Apply the generators of `word` (last element first) to the seed."""
    t = SEED
    for idx in reversed(word):
        m = MATRICES[idx]
        a, b, c = t
        t = (m[0][0] * a + m[0][1] * b + m[0][2] * c,
             m[1][0] * a + m[1][1] * b + m[1][2] * c,
             m[2][0] * a + m[2][1] * b + m[2][2] * c)
    return t

from __future__ import annotations

from math import isqrt, pi
from typing import List

def mobius_table(N: int) -> List[int]:
    """Moebius function mu(1..N) by a linear-ish sieve.  O(N log log N)."""
    mu = [1] * (N + 1)
    primes: List[int] = []
    is_comp = [False] * (N + 1)
    for i in range(2, N + 1):
        if not is_comp[i]:
            primes.append(i)
            mu[i] = -1
        for p in primes:
            if i * p > N:
                break
            is_comp[i * p] = True
            if i % p == 0:
                mu[i * p] = 0
                break
            mu[i * p] = -mu[i]
    return mu


def wedge_opposite_parity(T: int) -> int:
    """#{(n, m) : 0 < n < m, n + m odd, m^2 + n^2 <= T}.

    Summing over m and counting the admissible n by parity in closed form makes
    this an O(sqrt(T)) computation with no gcd calls.
    """
    total = 0
    mmax = isqrt(T)
    for m in range(2, mmax + 1):
        nmax = min(m - 1, isqrt(T - m * m))
        if nmax < 1:
            continue
        # count n in [1, nmax] with parity opposite to m
        if m % 2 == 0:
            total += (nmax + 1) // 2      # odd n
        else:
            total += nmax // 2            # even n
    return total


def count_pair_box(H: int) -> int:
    """#Q(H) = #{(n,m): 0<n<m, gcd(n,m)=1, n+m odd, m^2+n^2 <= H} = #B(H).

    Moebius inversion removes the visibility (coprimality) condition:

        #Q(H) = sum_{d odd} mu(d) * #{(n,m): 0<n<m, n+m odd, d|n, d|m,
                                              m^2+n^2 <= H}
              = sum_{d odd} mu(d) * wedge_opposite_parity(H / d^2),

    where only odd d contribute, since an even common divisor would make both
    entries even and destroy the opposite-parity condition.

    Complexity: sum over d <= sqrt(H) of O(sqrt(H)/d) = O(sqrt(H) log H) time,
    O(sqrt(H)) memory -- against O(H) for direct enumeration.
    """
    D = isqrt(H)
    mu = mobius_table(D)
    total = 0
    for d in range(1, D + 1, 2):
        if mu[d]:
            total += mu[d] * wedge_opposite_parity(H // (d * d))
    return total

from __future__ import annotations

from math import isqrt, log, sqrt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]

B1 = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
B2 = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
B3 = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))
SEED: Triple = (3, 4, 5)
H: int = 200000


def apply_matrix(m, t: Triple) -> Triple:
    a, b, c = t
    return (m[0][0]*a + m[0][1]*b + m[0][2]*c,
            m[1][0]*a + m[1][1]*b + m[1][2]*c,
            m[2][0]*a + m[2][1]*b + m[2][2]*c)


depths: Dict[int, int] = {}
stack: List[Tuple[Triple, int]] = [(SEED, 0)]
while stack:
    t, d = stack.pop()
    if t[2] > H:
        continue
    depths[d] = depths.get(d, 0) + 1
    for M in (B1, B2, B3):
        stack.append((apply_matrix(M, t), d + 1))

ds = sorted(depths)
counts = [depths[d] for d in ds]
total = sum(counts)
mean_depth = sum(d * depths[d] for d in ds) / total

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5))

            label=f"max depth = {max(ds)}  ($\\sqrt{{H}}/2$ = {isqrt(H)/2:.0f})")
ax1.set_yscale("log")

ax1.set_ylabel("number of nodes inside the box")
ax1.set_title(f"Depth profile of the tree in $[1,H]^3$, $H = {H}$\n"
              f"({total} nodes: dense logarithmic bulk, long parabolic tail)")
ax1.legend(fontsize=9)

ks = np.arange(0, 26)
para = 4 * (ks + 1.0) ** 2 + 1
hyper = [5.0]
for _ in ks[:-1]:
    hyper.append(hyper[-1] * (3 + 2 * sqrt(2)))
ax2.semilogy(ks, para, "o-", c="#2a9d8f",
             label=r"parabolic spine $B_3^k$:  $c_k = 4(k+1)^2+1$")
ax2.semilogy(ks, hyper, "s-", c="#c1121f",
             label=r"hyperbolic branch $B_2^k$:  $c_k \approx 5(3+2\sqrt{2})^k$")
ax2.axhline(H, color="k", ls="--", lw=0.9, label=f"box height $H = {H}$")
ax2.set_xlabel("depth $k$")
ax2.set_ylabel("hypotenuse $c_k$")
ax2.set_title("Two speeds of growth along the generators")
ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
ax2.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.25)

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("berggren_depth.png", dpi=150)
print("wrote berggren_depth.png")

    for(const [n,m,k] of pts){
      if(k===0 || k===1){ if(!els.showOther.checked) continue; }

    els.pick.innerHTML =
      `(n, m) = (${nn}, ${mm})  <span class="tag">visible, opposite parity</span><br>` +
      `triangle (a, b, c) = <b class="hot">(${fmt(a)}, ${fmt(b)}, ${fmt(c)})</b><br>` +
      `check: ${a}² + ${b}² = ${a*a+b*b} = ${c}²<br>` +
      `built from (3,4,5) by  <span class="acc">${w}</span>  (depth ${address(a,b,c).length})`;
  });

  hsl.addEventListener('input', refresh);
  els.showOther.addEventListener('change', draw);
  els.showRays.addEventListener('change', draw);
  refresh();
})();

  "interactive_layout": "# A Tree That Grows Every Right Triangle

### How three matrices, one seed, and a quarter of a circle explain why perfect right triangles are both everywhere and almost nowhere

---

## 1. The puzzle in one picture

Try to draw a right triangle on graph paper whose three sides are all whole numbers. Almost every triangle you draw will have an irrational hypotenuse. The famous ones — $3,4,5$ and $5,12,13$ — look like lucky accidents.

They are not. They are the nodes of a single tree, and by the end of this page you will be able to reach *any* of them by clicking three buttons, know exactly how many of them fit in a box, and know why the answer involves $\pi$.

Here are the three questions we will answer, all of them sharp:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What fraction of the $H^3$ integer triples $(a,b,c)$ with $1\le a,b,c\le H$ are right triangles reachable from $(3,4,5)$? | A vanishing fraction, $O(1/H^2)$ |
| How many are there, exactly? | $\Theta(H)$ — provably between $H/100$ and $H$, and in truth $\approx H/(2\pi)$ |
| What fraction of the *primitive right triangles* in the box does the tree capture? | **All of them.** Exactly $1$, not $1-o(1)$ |

---

## 2. The three matrices

Write a triangle as the column vector $(a,b,c)$, with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$. Berggren's three matrices are

$$
B_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_3 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Feed them the seed:
$B_1(3,4,5) = (5,12,13)$, $B_2(3,4,5)=(21,20,29)$, $B_3(3,4,5)=(15,8,17)$. All three are right triangles again. Apply them once more and you get nine; then twenty-seven; forever.

**Go and play.** Climb the tree, watch each node get verified live, and use the descent panel to see the tree *reverse itself* — that reversal is the entire proof that nothing is missing.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: why every child is again a primitive right triangle</b></summary>

Four things must hold, and each is a short check.

**The Pythagorean identity.** Expand, for instance for $B_2$:
$$(a+2b+2c)^2+(2a+b+2c)^2-(2a+2b+3c)^2 \;=\; -a^2-b^2+c^2,$$
which vanishes precisely when $a^2+b^2=c^2$. The same computation, with signs adjusted, works for $B_1$ and $B_3$.

**Positivity.** For a positive right triangle one has $c<a+b$ (square both sides: $c^2 = a^2+b^2 < (a+b)^2$) and $a<c$, $b<c$. Substituting these three facts makes every coordinate of every child a manifestly positive combination.

**Primitivity.** Each $B_i$ has determinant $\pm 1$, so $B_i^{-1}$ has integer entries too. A common divisor of the child's coordinates therefore divides the parent's, and conversely — coprimality transfers in both directions.

**Parity.** If $a$ is odd and the triple is primitive, then $b$ is even and $c$ is odd. Each child's first coordinate is $\pm a + 2b + 2c$, which is odd again.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the descent, and why nothing is missing</b></summary>

Given a positive primitive right triangle $(a,b,c)$ with $a$ odd, other than the seed, form the three *parent forms*
$$u = a+2b-2c, \qquad v = 2a+b-2c, \qquad w = 3c-2a-2b .$$

*Step 1: $0 < w < c$.* The upper bound is $c<a+b$. For the lower bound, $4(a+b)^2 = 4(c^2+2ab) \le 8c^2 < 9c^2$, using $2ab \le a^2+b^2=c^2$; hence $2(a+b)<3c$.

*Step 2: $u$ and $v$ are never both $\le 0$.* Suppose $u\le0$, i.e. $a\le 2(c-b)$. Squaring (legitimate since $b<c$) gives $c^2-b^2\le4(c-b)^2$; dividing by $c-b>0$ leaves $c+b\le4(c-b)$, i.e. $5b\le3c$. Symmetrically $v\le0$ forces $5a\le3c$. Both together would give $25c^2 = 25(a^2+b^2)\le 18c^2$ — absurd.

*Step 3: the sign pattern names the parent.* $u=0$ would make $a$ even; $v=0$ happens only for the seed. So $(\operatorname{sgn} u, \operatorname{sgn} v)$ is one of $(+,-), (+,+), (-,+)$, corresponding to $B_1, B_2, B_3$, and $(|u|,|v|,w)$ is again a positive primitive triangle with odd first leg.

*Step 4: terminate.* The hypotenuse strictly drops at every step, and hypotenuses are positive integers, so the descent halts — and the only place it can halt is the seed. Reading the steps backwards writes the triangle as a word in $B_1,B_2,B_3$.

Two different words never give the same triangle either, so the address is unique: the tree is *free*.

</details>

---

## 3. Now draw a box

Fix $H$ and look at the cube of integer points $\{1,\dots,H\}^3$, which holds $H^3$ triples. How many are tree triangles?

The proved answer, sharp on both sides:

$$\frac{H}{100} \;\le\; \#\{\text{tree triangles in the box}\} \;\le\; \min\left(4H,\ \left(\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor + 1\right)^2\right) \qquad (H \ge 5).$$

The upper bound comes from a two-line trick worth savouring. If $(a,b,c)$ is primitive with $a$ odd then $c+a = 2m^2$ and $c-a = 2n^2$ for integers $m,n$. So the map $(a,b,c)\mapsto(c+a,\,c-a)$ sends every tree triangle to a **pair of doubled squares** — and it is injective, because $c+a$ and $c-a$ recover $a$ and $c$, and then $b^2 = c^2-a^2$ fixes $b$. With $c\le H$ both $m$ and $n$ are at most $\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor$. Two subtractions have collapsed a three-dimensional count to a two-dimensional one.

Since the box has $H^3$ points and the tree contributes at most $4H$ of them:

$$\frac{\#\{\text{tree triangles in the box}\}}{H^3} \;\le\; \frac{4}{H} \;\longrightarrow\; 0 .$$

Perfect right triangles are **vanishingly rare** in the box. At $H = 20\,000$ there are $3186$ of them among $8\times10^{12}$ lattice points.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 4. The twist: rare, but complete

Rare among all triples — but that is the less interesting comparison. What about the primitive right triangles themselves?

Here the tree does not merely capture *most* of them. It captures **all** of them.

The reason is a parity fact. In a primitive right triangle exactly one leg is odd: both legs cannot be even (they are coprime), and both cannot be odd, since then $c^2 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ and no square is $2$ mod $4$. The tree consists precisely of the triangles whose *first* leg is odd. So swapping the two legs is a perfect pairing between what the tree contains and what it does not:

> **Every primitive right triangle in the box is in the tree, or becomes a tree triangle after swapping its legs.** Counting ordered triples, $\#\{\text{primitive triples in the box}\} = 2\,\#\{\text{tree triangles in the box}\}$.

So the "$1-o(1)$" one might have expected is an exact $1$. As a set of *triangles*, with the legs unordered, the tree restricted to the box **is** the set of all primitive right triangles of hypotenuse at most $H$.

---

## 5. Where $\pi$ comes from

The proved bounds pin the density between $0.01$ and $1$. Computation says the truth is
$$\frac{\#\{\text{tree triangles in }[1,H]^3\}}{H} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2\pi} = 0.15915494\ldots$$

Why on earth $\pi$? Because the counting problem is *exactly* — a bijection, not an estimate — a lattice-point problem in a circular wedge. Play with it:

{{interactive_demo:0}}

The dictionary is Euclid's: the pair $(n,m)$ corresponds to the triangle $(m^2-n^2,\,2mn,\,m^2+n^2)$, and the box condition $c\le H$ becomes $m^2+n^2\le H$. Primitivity of the triangle becomes **visibility** of the point $(n,m)$ from the origin (that is, $\gcd(n,m)=1$: nothing blocks the line of sight), and oddness of the first leg becomes **opposite parity** of $n$ and $m$.

Three densities then multiply:

$$\underbrace{\frac{\pi H}{8}}_{\text{area of the wedge}} \times \underbrace{\frac{6}{\pi^2}}_{\text{visible}} \times \underbrace{\frac{2}{3}}_{\text{opposite parity}} \;=\; \frac{H}{2\pi}.$$

The $\pi$ upstairs is the circle; the $\pi^2$ downstairs is $\zeta(2)$, the coprimality density; the $2/3$ is the parity filter, because among coprime pairs the three classes (odd,odd), (odd,even), (even,odd) are equally common. Everything cancels to $1/(2\pi)$.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the conjecture, and exactly which constants the proof throws away</b></summary>

**Conjecture.** $\#\{\text{tree triangles in }[1,H]^3\} = \dfrac{H}{2\pi} + O(\sqrt H \log H)$.

The bijection is exact and unconditional, so what remains is a Möbius-weighted [Gauss circle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_circle_problem) for the wedge: the main term is routine, and the error requires uniform control of the lattice-point discrepancy for discs of radius $\sqrt H/d$, summed against $\mu(d)$.

Where does the proved upper bound lose its factor? It bounds the wedge by the full square $[0,\sqrt H]^2$ (a loss of $8/\pi$), ignores coprimality (a loss of $\pi^2/6$), and ignores parity (a loss of $3/2$). Their product is
$$\frac{8}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{2} = 2\pi,$$
which is precisely the observed gap. The two-square trick is exactly $2\pi$ too generous — a satisfying audit.

</details>

---

## 6. Two speeds of growth

The three matrices do not grow triangles at the same rate, and this is why the tree looks so lopsided.

$B_2$ is **hyperbolic**: it multiplies the hypotenuse by more than $5$ every time, the exact factor being the silver-ratio square $3+2\sqrt2 = 5.8284\ldots$. The pure-$B_2$ branch has hypotenuses $5, 29, 169, 985, 5741, 33461,\dots$ — alternate [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number), carrying the triangles whose legs differ by one.

$B_3$ is **unipotent** — parabolic, with $1$ as its only eigenvalue. It preserves $c-a$, and its orbit of the seed is beautifully explicit:
$$B_3^{\,k}(3,4,5) = \bigl(4(k+1)^2-1,\ 4(k+1),\ 4(k+1)^2+1\bigr) = (3,4,5), (15,8,17), (35,12,37), (63,16,65),\ldots$$
The hypotenuse grows only *quadratically* in the depth. So inside a box of height $H$ the tree reaches depth $\sim\sqrt H$, while a generic node at depth $d$ already has hypotenuse up to $5\cdot6^d$.

{{visualization:2}}

The result is a dense exponential bush with a few very long, very thin whiskers: at $H = 200\,000$ the tree holds $31\,819$ triangles of *mean* depth $17$, and its deepest node sits at depth $314$.

---

## 7. Computing with it

Three algorithms fall out of the structure, each exploiting a different theorem.

The tree walk is possible only because the tree is free (no duplicates to detect) and every generator increases the hypotenuse (so pruning is safe):

{{algorithm:0}}

The descent turns the completeness proof into a decoder: it computes the unique address of any primitive triangle you hand it.

{{algorithm:1}}

And the bijection with the wedge lets us count *without enumerating*: a Möbius sieve on the visibility condition brings the cost down from $O(H)$ to $O(\sqrt H \log H)$, which is what makes the $H = 10^9$ data point below feasible in a fraction of a second.

{{algorithm:2}}

## 9. What to take away

A set defined by a **rule of generation** (apply these matrices, starting here) turned out to coincide with a set defined by a **property** (primitive, Pythagorean, odd first leg). Once you know that, the counting question migrates into geometry, becomes a question about visible lattice points in a disc, and $\pi$ walks in unannounced.

Three answers, all correct, to "how common are Pythagorean triples?":

- Among all integer triples in a box: **vanishingly rare**, a fraction $O(1/H^2)$.
- Counted against the height: **exactly $\Theta(H)$**, with density approaching $1/(2\pi)$.
- Among primitive Pythagorean triples: **all of them**, no exceptions, up to swapping the legs.

Rarity and completeness are not in conflict. They answer different questions — and knowing which question you are asking is, as usual, most of the mathematics.

* `bergBox_density_tendsto_zero` : `#(bergBox H) / H³ → 0`, i.e. Berggren-generated
  triples are a vanishing proportion of all triples in the box;
* `bergBox_eq_ppOddBox` and `card_ppBox_eq_two_mul_card_bergBox` : the Berggren tree
  captures *exactly* the primitive Pythagorean triples of the box with odd first leg,
  hence exactly one half of all (ordered) primitive Pythagorean triples of the box and
  *all* of them up to swapping the two legs.  So the "`1 - o(1)`" proportion is in fact
  an exact `1`.
-/

namespace BerggrenBoxCounting

open BerggrenTree

/-- The full integer box `[1,H]³`. -/
def boxAll (H : ℕ) : Finset Tri :=
  Finset.Icc (1 : ℤ) (H : ℤ) ×ˢ Finset.Icc (1 : ℤ) (H : ℤ) ×ˢ Finset.Icc (1 : ℤ) (H : ℤ)

lemma mem_boxAll {H : ℕ} {t : Tri} :
    t ∈ boxAll H ↔ (1 ≤ t.1 ∧ t.1 ≤ H) ∧ (1 ≤ t.2.1 ∧ t.2.1 ≤ H) ∧ (1 ≤ t.2.2 ∧ t.2.2 ≤ H) := by
  simp [boxAll, Finset.mem_product, Finset.mem_Icc, and_assoc]

open Classical in
/-- The Berggren-generated triples inside the box `[1,H]³`. -/
noncomputable def bergBox (H : ℕ) : Finset Tri := (boxAll H).filter (fun t => Reach t)

open Classical in
/-- All primitive Pythagorean triples inside the box `[1,H]³`. -/
noncomputable def ppBox (H : ℕ) : Finset Tri :=
  (boxAll H).filter (fun t => t.1 ^ 2 + t.2.1 ^ 2 = t.2.2 ^ 2 ∧ Int.gcd t.1 t.2.1 = 1)

lemma mem_bergBox {H : ℕ} {t : Tri} :
    t ∈ bergBox H ↔ Reach t ∧ t.1 ≤ H ∧ t.2.1 ≤ H ∧ t.2.2 ≤ H := by
  classical
  rw [bergBox, Finset.mem_filter]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hbox, hr⟩
    obtain ⟨⟨_, h1⟩, ⟨_, h2⟩, ⟨_, h3⟩⟩ := mem_boxAll.mp hbox
    exact ⟨hr, h1, h2, h3⟩
  · rintro ⟨hr, h1, h2, h3⟩
    obtain ⟨ha, hb, hc, _, _, _⟩ := reach_valid hr
    exact ⟨mem_boxAll.mpr ⟨⟨by omega, h1⟩, ⟨by omega, h2⟩, ⟨by omega, h3⟩⟩, hr⟩

lemma mem_ppBox {H : ℕ} {t : Tri} :
    t ∈ ppBox H ↔ (1 ≤ t.1 ∧ t.1 ≤ H) ∧ (1 ≤ t.2.1 ∧ t.2.1 ≤ H) ∧ (1 ≤ t.2.2 ∧ t.2.2 ≤ H) ∧
      t.1 ^ 2 + t.2.1 ^ 2 = t.2.2 ^ 2 ∧ Int.gcd t.1 t.2.1 = 1 := by
  classical
  rw [ppBox, Finset.mem_filter]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hbox, hpy, hg⟩
    obtain ⟨h1, h2, h3⟩ := mem_boxAll.mp hbox
    exact ⟨h1, h2, h3, hpy, hg⟩
  · rintro ⟨h1, h2, h3, hpy, hg⟩
    exact ⟨mem_boxAll.mpr ⟨h1, h2, h3⟩, hpy, hg⟩

/-! ### The `(m,n)` parametrisation of a valid triple -/

/-- A positive primitive Pythagorean triple with odd first leg has `c + a = 2m²` and
`c - a = 2n²` for natural numbers `m, n`. -/
lemma valid_sq_decomposition {t : Tri} (h : Valid t) :
    ∃ M N : ℕ, t.2.2 + t.1 = 2 * (M : ℤ) ^ 2 ∧ t.2.2 - t.1 = 2 * (N : ℤ) ^ 2 := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c⟩ := t
  obtain ⟨ha, hb, hc, hpy, hgcd, hodd⟩ := h
  simp only at ha hb hc hpy hgcd hodd ⊢
  have hpt : PythagoreanTriple a b c := by
    unfold PythagoreanTriple
    linarith [hpy]
  obtain ⟨m, n, hab, hcc, _, _⟩ := PythagoreanTriple.coprime_classification.mp ⟨hpt, hgcd⟩
  have hcpos : c = m ^ 2 + n ^ 2 := by
    rcases hcc with h | h
    · exact h
    · exfalso
      nlinarith [sq_nonneg m, sq_nonneg n]
  have ha' : a = m ^ 2 - n ^ 2 := by
    rcases hab with ⟨h1, _⟩ | ⟨h1, _⟩
    · exact h1
    · exfalso
      have h2 : (2 : ℤ) ∣ a := ⟨m * n, by linarith [h1]⟩
      omega
  refine ⟨m.natAbs, n.natAbs, ?_, ?_⟩
  · have hM : ((m.natAbs : ℤ)) ^ 2 = m ^ 2 := Int.natAbs_pow_two m
    rw [hM, hcpos, ha']; ring
  · have hN : ((n.natAbs : ℤ)) ^ 2 = n ^ 2 := Int.natAbs_pow_two n
    rw [hN, hcpos, ha']; ring

/-! ### Upper bound -/

/-- **Sharp upper bound.**  The map `(a,b,c) ↦ (c+a, c-a)` sends a valid triple to a pair of
doubled squares, so the box contains at most `(⌊√H⌋+1)²` Berggren-generated triples. -/
theorem bergBox_card_le_sq_succ_sqrt (H : ℕ) :
    (bergBox H).card ≤ (Nat.sqrt H + 1) ^ 2 := by
  classical
  set s := Nat.sqrt H with hs
  set target : Finset (ℤ × ℤ) :=
    (Finset.Icc 0 s ×ˢ Finset.Icc 0 s).image (fun p => (2 * (p.1 : ℤ) ^ 2, 2 * (p.2 : ℤ) ^ 2))
    with htarget
  have hmap : ∀ t ∈ bergBox H, (t.2.2 + t.1, t.2.2 - t.1) ∈ target := by
    intro t ht
    obtain ⟨hr, h1, h2, h3⟩ := mem_bergBox.mp ht
    have hv := reach_valid hr
    obtain ⟨M, N, hM, hN⟩ := valid_sq_decomposition hv
    obtain ⟨ha, hb, hc, hpy, hgcd, hodd⟩ := hv
    have hMle : M ≤ s := by
      have : (M : ℤ) ^ 2 ≤ (H : ℤ) := by nlinarith [hM, ha, h3]
      have hMn : (M ^ 2 : ℕ) ≤ H := by exact_mod_cast this
      exact Nat.le_sqrt'.mpr (by nlinarith [hMn])
    have hNle : N ≤ s := by
      have : (N : ℤ) ^ 2 ≤ (H : ℤ) := by nlinarith [hN, ha, h3]
      have hNn : (N ^ 2 : ℕ) ≤ H := by exact_mod_cast this
      exact Nat.le_sqrt'.mpr (by nlinarith [hNn])
    refine Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(M, N), ?_, ?_⟩
    · simp only [Finset.mem_product, Finset.mem_Icc]
      exact ⟨⟨Nat.zero_le _, hMle⟩, Nat.zero_le _, hNle⟩
    · simp only [Prod.mk.injEq]
      exact ⟨hM.symm, hN.symm⟩
  have hinj : ∀ t ∈ bergBox H, ∀ t' ∈ bergBox H,
      (t.2.2 + t.1, t.2.2 - t.1) = (t'.2.2 + t'.1, t'.2.2 - t'.1) → t = t' := by
    intro t ht t' ht' heq
    obtain ⟨hr, _, _, _⟩ := mem_bergBox.mp ht
    obtain ⟨hr', _, _, _⟩ := mem_bergBox.mp ht'
    obtain ⟨ha, hb, hc, hpy, _, _⟩ := reach_valid hr
    obtain ⟨ha', hb', hc', hpy', _, _⟩ := reach_valid hr'
    simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at heq
    obtain ⟨e1, e2⟩ := heq
    have hA : t.1 = t'.1 := by omega
    have hC : t.2.2 = t'.2.2 := by omega
    have hB : t.2.1 = t'.2.1 := by nlinarith [hpy, hpy', hA, hC]
    exact Prod.ext hA (Prod.ext hB hC)
  have hcard : (bergBox H).card ≤ target.card :=
    Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn (fun t => (t.2.2 + t.1, t.2.2 - t.1)) hmap
      (fun t ht t' ht' h => hinj t ht t' ht' h)
  have htc : target.card ≤ (s + 1) ^ 2 := by
    refine le_trans (Finset.card_image_le) ?_
    simp [Finset.card_product, Nat.card_Icc, pow_two]
  exact le_trans hcard htc

/-- **Upper bound.**  At most `4H` triples of the box are Berggren-generated. -/
theorem bergBox_card_le (H : ℕ) (hH : 1 ≤ H) : (bergBox H).card ≤ 4 * H := by
  have hmain := bergBox_card_le_sq_succ_sqrt H
  have hsq : Nat.sqrt H ^ 2 ≤ H := Nat.sqrt_le' H
  have hs1 : 1 ≤ Nat.sqrt H := Nat.le_sqrt'.mpr (by simpa using hH)
  nlinarith

/-! ### Lower bound -/

/-- Turning a coprime opposite-parity pair into a primitive Pythagorean triple. -/
lemma pair_valid {n m : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hnm : n < m) (hg : Nat.gcd n m = 1)
    (hpar : (n + m) % 2 = 1) :
    Valid (((m : ℤ) ^ 2 - (n : ℤ) ^ 2, 2 * (m : ℤ) * (n : ℤ), (m : ℤ) ^ 2 + (n : ℤ) ^ 2)) := by
  have hn0 : (0 : ℤ) < (n : ℤ) := by exact_mod_cast hn
  have hnm' : ((n : ℤ)) < (m : ℤ) := by exact_mod_cast hnm
  have hm0 : (0 : ℤ) < (m : ℤ) := by linarith
  have hgz : Int.gcd (m : ℤ) (n : ℤ) = 1 := by
    rw [Int.gcd_natCast_natCast, Nat.gcd_comm]
    exact hg
  -- parity of `m` and `n`
  have hpar' : ((m : ℤ) % 2 = 0 ∧ (n : ℤ) % 2 = 1) ∨ ((m : ℤ) % 2 = 1 ∧ (n : ℤ) % 2 = 0) := by
    omega
  have hclass := PythagoreanTriple.coprime_classification (x := (m : ℤ) ^ 2 - (n : ℤ) ^ 2)
    (y := 2 * (m : ℤ) * (n : ℤ)) (z := (m : ℤ) ^ 2 + (n : ℤ) ^ 2)
  obtain ⟨hpt, hgcd⟩ := hclass.mpr ⟨(m : ℤ), (n : ℤ),
    Or.inl ⟨rfl, rfl⟩, Or.inl rfl, hgz, hpar'⟩
  have hpy : ((m : ℤ) ^ 2 - (n : ℤ) ^ 2) ^ 2 + (2 * (m : ℤ) * (n : ℤ)) ^ 2
      = ((m : ℤ) ^ 2 + (n : ℤ) ^ 2) ^ 2 := by ring
  refine ⟨by simp only; nlinarith, by simp only; positivity, by simp only; positivity, hpy,
    hgcd, ?_⟩
  -- the first leg is odd
  simp only
  rcases hpar' with ⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩
  · obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k : ℤ, (m : ℤ) = 2 * k := ⟨(m : ℤ) / 2, by omega⟩
    obtain ⟨l, hl⟩ : ∃ l : ℤ, (n : ℤ) = 2 * l + 1 := ⟨((n : ℤ) - 1) / 2, by omega⟩
    have : (m : ℤ) ^ 2 - (n : ℤ) ^ 2 = 2 * (2 * k ^ 2 - 2 * l ^ 2 - 2 * l) - 1 := by
      rw [hk, hl]; ring
    omega
  · obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k : ℤ, (m : ℤ) = 2 * k + 1 := ⟨((m : ℤ) - 1) / 2, by omega⟩
    obtain ⟨l, hl⟩ : ∃ l : ℤ, (n : ℤ) = 2 * l := ⟨(n : ℤ) / 2, by omega⟩
    have : (m : ℤ) ^ 2 - (n : ℤ) ^ 2 = 2 * (2 * k ^ 2 + 2 * k - 2 * l ^ 2) + 1 := by
      rw [hk, hl]; ring
    omega

/-- **Lower bound.**  At least `H / 100` triples of the box are Berggren-generated. -/
theorem bergBox_card_ge (H : ℕ) (hH : 5 ≤ H) : H ≤ 100 * (bergBox H).card := by
  classical
  set X := Nat.sqrt (H / 2) with hX
  -- the injection from coprime opposite-parity pairs
  have hmap : ∀ p ∈ CoprimePairDensity.copOpp X,
      (((p.2 : ℤ) ^ 2 - (p.1 : ℤ) ^ 2, 2 * (p.2 : ℤ) * (p.1 : ℤ),
        (p.2 : ℤ) ^ 2 + (p.1 : ℤ) ^ 2) : Tri) ∈ bergBox H := by
    rintro ⟨n, m⟩ hp
    obtain ⟨hn1, hnX, hm1, hmX, hgcd, hnm, hpar⟩ := CoprimePairDensity.mem_copOpp.mp hp
    simp only at hn1 hnX hm1 hmX hgcd hnm hpar
    have hval := pair_valid hn1 hnm hgcd hpar
    have hsum : m ^ 2 + n ^ 2 ≤ H := by
      have h1 : X ^ 2 ≤ H / 2 := Nat.sqrt_le' (H / 2)
      have h2 : m ^ 2 ≤ X ^ 2 := Nat.pow_le_pow_left hmX 2
      have h3 : n ^ 2 ≤ X ^ 2 := Nat.pow_le_pow_left hnX 2
      omega
    have hsumZ : ((m : ℤ)) ^ 2 + ((n : ℤ)) ^ 2 ≤ (H : ℤ) := by exact_mod_cast hsum
    have hn0 : (0 : ℤ) < (n : ℤ) := by exact_mod_cast hn1
    have hnm' : ((n : ℤ)) < (m : ℤ) := by exact_mod_cast hnm
    refine mem_bergBox.mpr ⟨reach_iff_valid _ |>.mpr hval, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · simp only; nlinarith
    · simp only; nlinarith
    · simpa using hsumZ
  have hinj : ∀ p ∈ CoprimePairDensity.copOpp X, ∀ q ∈ CoprimePairDensity.copOpp X,
      (((p.2 : ℤ) ^ 2 - (p.1 : ℤ) ^ 2, 2 * (p.2 : ℤ) * (p.1 : ℤ),
        (p.2 : ℤ) ^ 2 + (p.1 : ℤ) ^ 2) : Tri)
        = (((q.2 : ℤ) ^ 2 - (q.1 : ℤ) ^ 2, 2 * (q.2 : ℤ) * (q.1 : ℤ),
        (q.2 : ℤ) ^ 2 + (q.1 : ℤ) ^ 2) : Tri) → p = q := by
    rintro ⟨n, m⟩ _ ⟨n', m'⟩ _ heq
    simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at heq
    obtain ⟨e1, _, e3⟩ := heq
    have hm : ((m : ℤ)) ^ 2 = ((m' : ℤ)) ^ 2 := by linarith
    have hn : ((n : ℤ)) ^ 2 = ((n' : ℤ)) ^ 2 := by linarith
    have hmn : m ^ 2 = m' ^ 2 := by exact_mod_cast hm
    have hnn : n ^ 2 = n' ^ 2 := by exact_mod_cast hn
    have : m = m' := Nat.pow_left_injective (by norm_num) hmn
    have : n = n' := Nat.pow_left_injective (by norm_num) hnn
    simp_all
  have hcard : (CoprimePairDensity.copOpp X).card ≤ (bergBox H).card :=
    Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn _ hmap (fun p hp q hq h => hinj p hp q hq h)
  -- the root is in the box, so the box is non-empty
  have hroot : ((3 : ℤ), (4 : ℤ), (5 : ℤ)) ∈ bergBox H := by
    have h5 : (5 : ℤ) ≤ (H : ℤ) := by exact_mod_cast hH
    refine mem_bergBox.mpr ⟨Reach.root, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> simp only <;> omega
  have hne : 1 ≤ (bergBox H).card := Finset.card_pos.mpr ⟨_, hroot⟩
  -- quantitative chain
  have hdens := CoprimePairDensity.card_copOpp_ge X
  have hX1 : 1 ≤ X := by
    rw [hX]
    exact Nat.le_sqrt'.mpr (by omega)
  have hXsq : H / 2 ≤ 3 * X ^ 2 := by
    have h1 : H / 2 < (X + 1) ^ 2 := Nat.lt_succ_sqrt' (H / 2)
    nlinarith
  have hH2 : H ≤ 2 * (H / 2) + 1 := by omega
  nlinarith [hdens, hcard, hne, hXsq, hH2]

/-! ### Vanishing density in the full box -/

/-- **Berggren-generated triples are a vanishing proportion of the box.** -/
theorem bergBox_density_tendsto_zero :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun H : ℕ => ((bergBox H).card : ℝ) / (H : ℝ) ^ 3) Filter.atTop
      (nhds 0) := by
  have hbound : ∀ᶠ H : ℕ in Filter.atTop,
      ((bergBox H).card : ℝ) / (H : ℝ) ^ 3 ≤ 4 / (H : ℝ) := by
    filter_upwards [Filter.eventually_ge_atTop 1] with H hH
    have hHR : (1 : ℝ) ≤ (H : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hH
    have hcard : ((bergBox H).card : ℝ) ≤ 4 * (H : ℝ) := by
      exact_mod_cast bergBox_card_le H hH
    rw [div_le_div_iff₀ (by positivity) (by positivity)]
    have h1 : ((bergBox H).card : ℝ) * (H : ℝ) ≤ 4 * (H : ℝ) * (H : ℝ) := by nlinarith
    have hcube : (H : ℝ) ^ 3 = (H : ℝ) * (H : ℝ) * (H : ℝ) := by ring
    have h2 : (4 : ℝ) * (H : ℝ) * (H : ℝ) ≤ 4 * (H : ℝ) ^ 3 := by
      rw [hcube]; nlinarith
    linarith
  have hnn : ∀ᶠ H : ℕ in Filter.atTop, (0 : ℝ) ≤ ((bergBox H).card : ℝ) / (H : ℝ) ^ 3 := by
    filter_upwards [Filter.eventually_ge_atTop 1] with H _
    positivity
  refine tendsto_of_tendsto_of_tendsto_of_le_of_le' tendsto_const_nhds ?_ hnn hbound
  exact tendsto_const_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat 4

/-! ### Comparison with the primitive Pythagorean triples of the box -/

open Classical in
/-- Primitive Pythagorean triples of the box whose first leg is odd. -/
noncomputable def ppOddBox (H : ℕ) : Finset Tri := (ppBox H).filter (fun t => t.1 % 2 = 1)

/-- **The Berggren tree captures exactly the odd-first-leg primitive Pythagorean triples
of the box.** -/
theorem bergBox_eq_ppOddBox (H : ℕ) : bergBox H = ppOddBox H := by
  classical
  ext t
  rw [ppOddBox, Finset.mem_filter]
  constructor
  · intro ht
    obtain ⟨hr, h1, h2, h3⟩ := mem_bergBox.mp ht
    obtain ⟨ha, hb, hc, hpy, hgcd, hodd⟩ := reach_valid hr
    exact ⟨mem_ppBox.mpr ⟨⟨by omega, h1⟩, ⟨by omega, h2⟩, ⟨by omega, h3⟩, hpy, hgcd⟩, hodd⟩
  · rintro ⟨hpp, hodd⟩
    obtain ⟨⟨ha1, ha2⟩, ⟨hb1, hb2⟩, ⟨hc1, hc2⟩, hpy, hgcd⟩ := mem_ppBox.mp hpp
    refine mem_bergBox.mpr ⟨?_, ha2, hb2, hc2⟩
    exact (reach_iff_valid t).mpr ⟨by omega, by omega, by omega, hpy, hgcd, hodd⟩

/-- In a primitive Pythagorean triple exactly one leg is odd, so swapping the legs is a
bijection between the odd-first-leg and even-first-leg triples of the box. -/
theorem card_ppBox_eq_two_mul_card_bergBox (H : ℕ) :
    (ppBox H).card = 2 * (bergBox H).card := by
  classical
  have hsplit : (ppOddBox H).card + ((ppBox H).filter (fun t => ¬ t.1 % 2 = 1)).card
      = (ppBox H).card := by
    rw [ppOddBox]
    exact Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not _
  have hswap1 : ((ppBox H).filter (fun t => ¬ t.1 % 2 = 1)).card ≤ (ppOddBox H).card := by
    refine Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn (fun t => (t.2.1, t.1, t.2.2)) ?_ ?_
    · intro t ht
      obtain ⟨hpp, heven⟩ := Finset.mem_filter.mp ht
      obtain ⟨⟨ha1, ha2⟩, ⟨hb1, hb2⟩, ⟨hc1, hc2⟩, hpy, hgcd⟩ := mem_ppBox.mp hpp
      have hbodd : t.2.1 % 2 = 1 := by
        rcases Int.emod_two_eq_zero_or_one t.1 with h1 | h1
        · rcases Int.emod_two_eq_zero_or_one t.2.1 with h2 | h2
          · exfalso
            have hd1 : (2 : ℤ) ∣ t.1 := by omega
            have hd2 : (2 : ℤ) ∣ t.2.1 := by omega
            have := (Int.isCoprime_iff_gcd_eq_one.mpr hgcd).isUnit_of_dvd' hd1 hd2
            have := Int.isUnit_iff.1 this
            omega
          · exact h2
        · exact absurd h1 heven
      refine Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨mem_ppBox.mpr ⟨⟨hb1, hb2⟩, ⟨ha1, ha2⟩, ⟨hc1, hc2⟩, ?_, ?_⟩,
        hbodd⟩
      · simp only; linarith [hpy]
      · simp only; rwa [Int.gcd_comm]
    · intro t _ t' _ heq
      simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at heq
      exact Prod.ext heq.2.1 (Prod.ext heq.1 heq.2.2)
  have hswap2 : (ppOddBox H).card ≤ ((ppBox H).filter (fun t => ¬ t.1 % 2 = 1)).card := by
    refine Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn (fun t => (t.2.1, t.1, t.2.2)) ?_ ?_
    · intro t ht
      obtain ⟨hpp, hodd⟩ := Finset.mem_filter.mp ht
      obtain ⟨⟨ha1, ha2⟩, ⟨hb1, hb2⟩, ⟨hc1, hc2⟩, hpy, hgcd⟩ := mem_ppBox.mp hpp
      have hbeven : ¬ t.2.1 % 2 = 1 := by
        intro h2
        have hc2' : t.2.2 ^ 2 % 4 = 2 := by
          obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k : ℤ, t.1 = 2 * k + 1 := ⟨(t.1 - 1) / 2, by omega⟩
          obtain ⟨l, hl⟩ : ∃ l : ℤ, t.2.1 = 2 * l + 1 := ⟨(t.2.1 - 1) / 2, by omega⟩
          have : t.2.2 ^ 2 = 4 * (k ^ 2 + k + l ^ 2 + l) + 2 := by
            rw [← hpy, hk, hl]; ring
          omega
        obtain ⟨j, hj⟩ : ∃ j : ℤ, t.2.2 = 2 * j ∨ t.2.2 = 2 * j + 1 :=
          ⟨t.2.2 / 2, by omega⟩
        rcases hj with hj | hj
        · have : t.2.2 ^ 2 = 4 * j ^ 2 := by rw [hj]; ring
          omega
        · have : t.2.2 ^ 2 = 4 * (j ^ 2 + j) + 1 := by rw [hj]; ring
          omega
      refine Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨mem_ppBox.mpr ⟨⟨hb1, hb2⟩, ⟨ha1, ha2⟩, ⟨hc1, hc2⟩, ?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
      · simp only; linarith [hpy]
      · simp only; rwa [Int.gcd_comm]
      · simpa using hbeven
    · intro t _ t' _ heq
      simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at heq
      exact Prod.ext heq.2.1 (Prod.ext heq.1 heq.2.2)
  rw [bergBox_eq_ppOddBox]
  omega

/-- Since both legs of a Pythagorean triple are smaller than the hypotenuse, the box
condition is equivalent to a bound on the hypotenuse alone. -/

# Effective density of coprime pairs in a square, with parity refinement

This file proves a completely explicit, effective lower bound for the number of
coprime pairs `(n, m)` with `1 ≤ n < m ≤ X` and `n + m` odd:

    `11 * X^2 ≤ 144 * (copOpp X).card + 36`.

* the number of pairs in the square `[1,X]^2` is `X^2`;
* a pair whose gcd is `g ≥ 2` is `g` times a pair in `[1, X/g]^2`, so the number
  of *non*-coprime pairs is at most `∑_{g=2}^{X} ⌊X/g⌋^2 ≤ (25/36) X^2`,
  using `∑_{g ≥ 2} 1/g^2 ≤ 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/3 = 25/36`;
* symmetry (swapping the two coordinates) costs a factor `2`;
* pairs of two odd coprime numbers inject into opposite-parity coprime pairs via
  `(n, m) ↦ ((m-n)/2, (m+n)/2)`, costing another factor `2`.

and hence of Berggren-generated triples, in a box.

/-- All pairs in the square `[1,X] × [1,X]`. -/

lemma card_sq (X : ℕ) : (sq X).card = X ^ 2 := by
  simp [sq, Nat.card_Icc, pow_two]

/-- Coprime pairs in the square `[1,X] × [1,X]`. -/
def cop (X : ℕ) : Finset (ℕ × ℕ) := (sq X).filter (fun p => Nat.gcd p.1 p.2 = 1)

/-- Non-coprime pairs in the square `[1,X] × [1,X]`. -/
def bad (X : ℕ) : Finset (ℕ × ℕ) := (sq X).filter (fun p => ¬ (Nat.gcd p.1 p.2 = 1))

  rw [cop, bad, Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not, card_sq]

where `g` is its gcd. -/
lemma bad_subset (X : ℕ) :

  set g := Nat.gcd n m with hgdef

  have hgm : g ∣ m := Nat.gcd_dvd_right n m
  have hgpos : 0 < g := Nat.gcd_pos_of_pos_left _ hn1

  refine Finset.mem_image.2 ⟨(n / g, m / g), ?_, ?_⟩

grows the hypotenuse only quadratically ($4(k+1)^2+1$ along the spine from the seed), whereas $B_2$
multiplies it by the silver-ratio square $3+2\sqrt2$ at every step. What remains is to show that no
mixed word grows more slowly than the pure parabolic spine, which would pin the maximal depth, and to
prove that the depth of a uniformly random node of the box concentrates at $\Theta(\log H)$.

## Direction 3 — Sharper effective constants

Replacing the crude elementary sieve (which gives coprime density $\ge 11/36$ instead of the true
$6/\pi^2$) by an effective Möbius argument, and replacing the square-inscribed-in-a-disc step by a
direct wedge count, should narrow the proved interval for $\#\mathcal B(H)/H$ from $[1/100, 1]$ to
roughly $[0.14, 0.18]$ — bracketing the conjectural $1/(2\pi)$ from both sides with explicit
constants.

## Direction 4 — Other generating trees

The three Berggren matrices generate a free semigroup acting on a Diophantine set. Which other
triples of unimodular matrices give free covering trees of a Diophantine set, and does the
"$\Theta(H)$ with a computable constant" phenomenon persist? A classification of the seeds and
generator systems with this property would explain how special the Berggren system really is.

## Direction 5 — Counting by perimeter, area, or inradius

Counting by hypotenuse puts the parameters in a circular wedge. Counting by perimeter
$2m(m+n) \le P$ puts them inside a hyperbola-bounded region; counting by area or inradius gives yet
other shapes. In each case the density constant becomes an explicit integral over the corresponding
region times the same two Euler factors, and making these effective is a bounded and attractive
target.

## Direction 6 — Higher-dimensional analogues

Quaternionic or Lipschitz-integer trees generating primitive quadruples $a^2+b^2+c^2 = d^2$ admit
similar matrix descriptions. The corresponding box counts should be $\Theta(H^2)$, with an explicit
constant coming from a spherical shell rather than a circular wedge, and with a completeness theorem
proved by the same descent-on-the-hypotenuse technique.

    "demo": """"
Berggren-generated Pythagorean triples in a box: numerical demonstrations.

This self-contained script illustrates, with explicit computation, the results of
the accompanying paper:

  * The three Berggren matrices B1, B2, B3 acting on the seed (3,4,5) generate a
    ternary tree whose nodes are *exactly* the positive primitive Pythagorean
    triples (a,b,c) whose first leg a is odd.

  * Writing  bergBox(H) = { (a,b,c) in the tree : a,b,c <= H }, we have

        H / 100  <=  #bergBox(H)  <=  min( 4H, (floor(sqrt(H)) + 1)^2 )     (H >= 5)

    so #bergBox(H) = Theta(H); in particular #bergBox(H)/H^3 -> 0, i.e. tree
    triples are a vanishing fraction of the H^3 integer triples of the box.

  * #ppBox(H) = 2 * #bergBox(H), where ppBox(H) is the set of *all* ordered
    primitive Pythagorean triples in the box.  Hence the tree captures every
    primitive triple of the box up to swapping the two legs: the advertised
    proportion "1 - o(1)" is in fact exactly 1.

  * #bergBox(H) = #pairBox(H), the number of coprime, opposite-parity lattice
    points (n,m) with 0 < n < m and m^2 + n^2 <= H (a "visible point" count in a
    quarter disc).  Experimentally #bergBox(H)/H -> 1/(2*pi) = 0.159154...

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from math import gcd, isqrt, pi
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1. The three Berggren matrices
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

B1: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
B2: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
B3: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))

SEED: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


def apply_matrix(matrix: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...], t: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to a triple, returning the image triple."""
    a, b, c = t
    return tuple(row[0] * a + row[1] * b + row[2] * c for row in matrix)  # type: ignore[return-value]


def children(t: Triple) -> List[Triple]:
    """The three Berggren children of a triple."""
    return [apply_matrix(B1, t), apply_matrix(B2, t), apply_matrix(B3, t)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 2. Enumerating the tree inside a box
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def berg_box(H: int) -> List[Triple]:
    """All Berggren-generated triples (a,b,c) with 0 < a,b,c <= H.

    Because c > a and c > b for a Pythagorean triple, the box condition is just
    c <= H; and every Berggren step strictly increases c, so a depth-first search
    pruned at c > H is complete.
    """
    out: List[Triple] = []
    stack: List[Triple] = [SEED]
    while stack:
        t = stack.pop()
        if t[2] > H:
            continue
        out.append(t)
        stack.extend(children(t))
    return sorted(out)


def pp_box(H: int) -> List[Triple]:
    """All ordered primitive Pythagorean triples (a,b,c) with 0 < a,b,c <= H."""
    out: List[Triple] = []
    for c in range(1, H + 1):
        for a in range(1, c):
            b2 = c * c - a * a
            b = isqrt(b2)
            if b * b == b2 and 0 < b <= H and gcd(a, b) == 1:
                out.append((a, b, c))
    return sorted(out)


def pair_box(H: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Coprime opposite-parity pairs (n,m), 0 < n < m, with m^2 + n^2 <= H."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    mmax = isqrt(H)
    for m in range(2, mmax + 1):
        for n in range(1, m):
            if m * m + n * n <= H and gcd(n, m) == 1 and (n + m) % 2 == 1:
                out.append((n, m))
    return sorted(out)


def euclid(n: int, m: int) -> Triple:
    """Euclid's parametrisation: (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2)."""
    return (m * m - n * n, 2 * m * n, m * m + n * n)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 3. Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def show_tree(depth: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1.  The Berggren ternary tree rooted at (3,4,5)")
    print("=" * 74)
    level: List[Triple] = [SEED]
    for d in range(depth + 1):
        print(f"  depth {d}: " + ", ".join(str(t) for t in level[:9])
              + ("  ..." if len(level) > 9 else ""))
        nxt: List[Triple] = []
        for t in level:
            nxt.extend(children(t))
        level = nxt
    print()
    # every node is a primitive triple with odd first leg
    ok = all(
        a * a + b * b == c * c and gcd(a, b) == 1 and a % 2 == 1
        for a, b, c in berg_box(2000)
    )
    print(f"  every node with c <= 2000 is primitive Pythagorean with odd leg a: {ok}")
    print()


def show_counts(bounds: Tuple[int, ...] = (5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000, 20000)) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2.  Counting: Theta(H) bounds, the factor 2, and the lattice bijection")
    print("=" * 74)
    header = (f"{'H':>7} {'#berg':>7} {'H/100':>7} {'4H':>8} {'(sqrt+1)^2':>11} "
              f"{'#pp':>7} {'#pair':>7} {'#berg/H':>9} {'#berg/H^3':>11}")
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    for H in bounds:
        bb = berg_box(H)
        pb = pair_box(H)
        pp = pp_box(H) if H <= 5000 else None
        lo = H / 100.0
        hi1 = 4 * H
        hi2 = (isqrt(H) + 1) ** 2
        assert H <= 100 * len(bb), "lower bound violated"
        assert len(bb) <= min(hi1, hi2), "upper bound violated"
        assert len(bb) == len(pb), "lattice bijection violated"
        if pp is not None:
            assert len(pp) == 2 * len(bb), "factor-two identity violated"
        print(f"{H:>7} {len(bb):>7} {lo:>7.1f} {hi1:>8} {hi2:>11} "
              f"{(len(pp) if pp is not None else -1):>7} {len(pb):>7} "
              f"{len(bb)/H:>9.5f} {len(bb)/H**3:>11.3e}")
    print()
    print(f"  conjectured limit of #berg/H :  1/(2*pi) = {1/(2*pi):.6f}")
    print()


def show_bijection(H: int = 200) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3.  The bijection (n,m) -> (m^2-n^2, 2mn, m^2+n^2) with H =", H)
    print("=" * 74)
    pairs = pair_box(H)
    triples = set(berg_box(H))
    images = {euclid(n, m) for (n, m) in pairs}
    print(f"  #pairs = {len(pairs)},  #tree triples = {len(triples)},  "
          f"images = tree: {images == triples}")
    for (n, m) in pairs[:8]:
        print(f"    (n,m) = ({n},{m})  ->  {euclid(n, m)}")
    print()


def show_swap(H: int = 300) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4.  Every primitive triple of the box is in the tree up to a leg swap")
    print("=" * 74)
    tree = set(berg_box(H))
    bad = [t for t in pp_box(H) if t not in tree and (t[1], t[0], t[2]) not in tree]
    print(f"  H = {H}:  #pp = {len(pp_box(H))},  #tree = {len(tree)},  "
          f"exceptions = {len(bad)}")
    odd_first = [t for t in pp_box(H) if t[0] % 2 == 1]
    print(f"  primitive triples with odd first leg = {len(odd_first)} "
          f"= #tree ({len(tree)}): {len(odd_first) == len(tree)}")
    print()


def show_depth_profile(H: int = 100000) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5.  Depth profile: parabolic spine (quadratic) vs hyperbolic branch")
    print("=" * 74)
    # the B3-spine
    t: Triple = SEED
    spine: List[Triple] = [t]
    for _ in range(6):
        t = apply_matrix(B3, t)
        spine.append(t)
    print("  B3-spine from (3,4,5):")
    for k, s in enumerate(spine):
        print(f"    depth {k}: {s}   predicted c = 4(k+1)^2+1 = {4*(k+1)**2+1}")
    # the B2 branch
    t = SEED
    branch: List[Triple] = [t]
    for _ in range(6):
        t = apply_matrix(B2, t)
        branch.append(t)
    print("  B2-branch from (3,4,5): hypotenuses",
          [s[2] for s in branch], " (ratios ->", f"{3+2*math.sqrt(2):.4f})")
    # depth statistics inside the box
    depths: Dict[int, int] = {}
    stack: List[Tuple[Triple, int]] = [(SEED, 0)]
    maxdepth = 0
    total = 0
    weighted = 0
    while stack:
        u, d = stack.pop()
        if u[2] > H:
            continue
        depths[d] = depths.get(d, 0) + 1
        maxdepth = max(maxdepth, d)
        total += 1
        weighted += d
        for v in children(u):
            stack.append((v, d + 1))
    print(f"  H = {H}: nodes = {total}, max depth D(H) = {maxdepth} "
          f"(sqrt(H)/2 = {isqrt(H)/2:.1f}), mean depth = {weighted/total:.2f} "
          f"(log H = {math.log(H):.2f})")
    print()


def show_density_constant(H: int = 400000) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6.  Towards the Lehmer-type constant  #bergBox(H)/H -> 1/(2*pi)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'H':>8} {'#berg':>8} {'#berg/H':>10} {'1/(2pi)':>10} {'error*sqrt(H)':>15}")
    Hs = [H // 32, H // 16, H // 8, H // 4, H // 2, H]
    for h in Hs:
        c = len(pair_box(h))          # equal to #bergBox(h), by the bijection
        err = c / h - 1 / (2 * pi)
        print(f"{h:>8} {c:>8} {c/h:>10.6f} {1/(2*pi):>10.6f} "
              f"{err*math.sqrt(h):>15.4f}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    show_tree()
    show_counts()
    show_bijection()
    show_swap()
    show_depth_profile()
    show_density_constant()
    print("All assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

concept.title: Definability boundary for external interpretations
concept.concept_description:
**Conjecture.** An external interpretation is recoverable from structural truth exactly when it is constant on automorphism orbits and definable in the invariant language; for finite models, orbit constancy alone is sufficient after adding bounded counting modalities.

The key insight is that the meaning-collision example fails precisely because the interpretation does not factor through structural equivalence, suggesting orbit descent as the necessary condition and definability as the sufficient one.

**Why now?** The collision theorem provides the negative half of a classification problem, while finite orbit decompositions offer a direct route to testing the proposed converse.
